stem: Which part of a mouldboard plough lifts, turns and inverts the furrow slice?

options.content: The mouldboard
options.rationale: Correct: its curved surface turns the slice over.

options.content: The landside
options.rationale: The landside presses against the furrow wall.

options.content: The share
options.rationale: The share cuts the slice horizontally.

options.content: The hake
options.rationale: The hake is the hitch used for adjustment.

explanation: The share cuts, the mouldboard turns, the landside steadies.

stem: Which part of the plough cuts the furrow slice horizontally at the bottom?

options.content: The share
options.rationale: Correct: its point penetrates and its edge cuts.

options.content: The beam
options.rationale: The beam joins the parts.

options.content: The heel
options.rationale: The heel is the rear wearing end of the landside.

options.content: The handles
options.rationale: The handles are for steering.

explanation: A sharp share cuts cleanly and reduces draught.

stem: What is the function of the landside of a mouldboard plough?

options.content: To press against the furrow wall and keep the plough straight
options.rationale: Correct: it resists the sideways push of the soil.

options.content: To turn the furrow slice upside down
options.rationale: That is the mouldboard.

options.content: To cut the soil vertically in front of the share and the mouldboard
options.rationale: That is the coulter.

options.content: To attach the trek chain to the beam
options.rationale: That is the hake.

explanation: The landside balances the side thrust created as the mouldboard turns the soil.

stem: A farmer raises the wheel of his ox plough. What happens to the depth of ploughing?

options.content: The plough goes shallower
options.rationale: Lowering the wheel makes it shallower.

options.content: The plough goes deeper
options.rationale: Correct: the share sinks further below the wheel.

options.content: The depth stays the same but the width doubles
options.rationale: The wheel controls depth, not width.

options.content: The plough stops turning the soil
options.rationale: The mouldboard still turns the slice.

explanation: The wheel rides on the surface; raising it lets the body run deeper.

stem: Which implement is best for primary tillage of hard soil full of stones and old roots?

options.content: A spike-tooth harrow
options.rationale: A harrow is for secondary tillage.

options.content: A planter
options.rationale: A planter sows seed.

options.content: A ridger
options.rationale: A ridger forms ridges in prepared soil.

options.content: A disc plough
options.rationale: Correct: its rotating discs roll over obstacles.

explanation: Disc ploughs suit hard, stony, rooty or sticky soils where a mouldboard share would break or block.
hints: Which implement rolls rather than drags through the soil?

stem: Six weeks after planting, a farmer wants to remove weeds between rows of maize planted 90 cm apart. Which implement should he use?

options.content: A mouldboard plough pulled along each row
options.rationale: It would bury the crop.

options.content: A disc harrow
options.rationale: It would destroy the crop rows.

options.content: An inter-row cultivator set to the row width
options.rationale: Correct: its tines weed between rows.

options.content: A planter
options.rationale: A planter sows seed.

explanation: The cultivator's width is adjusted with the expanding lever to fit between the rows.

stem: Why should the share be sharpened or replaced when it becomes blunt and rounded?

options.content: A blunt share turns the furrow slice better
options.rationale: Turning depends on the mouldboard; bluntness only hurts.

options.content: A blunt share prevents rust during storage
options.rationale: Bluntness has nothing to do with rust.

options.content: A blunt share makes the whole plough lighter and easier to carry
options.rationale: Its mass hardly changes.

options.content: A blunt share raises the draught and will not stay in the ground
options.rationale: Correct: the animals tire and the furrow is shallow.

explanation: Sharp shares penetrate and cut easily, reducing draught and giving an even depth.

stem: After storage, Chipo's plough mouldboard is badly rusted and the furrow slice now sticks to it instead of turning cleanly. Which practice would have prevented this?

options.content: Storing the plough upright in the open field
options.rationale: Rain would cause even more rust.

options.content: Loosening every nut and bolt before storing it
options.rationale: Loose bolts do not stop rust.

options.content: Coating bright surfaces with used oil or grease before storage
options.rationale: Correct: a rust-free polished surface scours soil cleanly.

options.content: Painting the share and mouldboard with whitewash before storage
options.rationale: Whitewash does not stop rust on working surfaces.

explanation: Clean, oil and store under cover; rough rusty mouldboards let soil stick.
hints: What protects bare steel from moisture?

stem: A ridger has two mouldboards (wings) that throw soil to both sides.
explanation: True. The double mouldboard forms ridges and is used for earthing up.

stem: Fertiliser should be left in a planter's hopper at the end of the day so that it is ready next morning.
explanation: False. Fertiliser absorbs moisture, cakes and corrodes the metal, so the hopper is emptied and cleaned.

stem: Match each part of the mouldboard plough with its function.

right.content: Hitch for adjusting depth and width
Used to steer and lift the plough
Main bar that carries the pull to the body
Body to which share, mouldboard and landside are bolted
Replaceable rear wearing part of the landside

explanation: Know each part's position and job.

stem: Match each implement with its main use.

right.content: Break clods and level the seedbed
Place seed at even depth and spacing

explanation: Each implement does a different job.

stem: Complete the sentence.

payload.template: On an ox plough the depth is adjusted using the {{blank:a}} and the vertical holes of the hake; the width is adjusted using the {{blank:b}} holes of the hake.

explanation: Wheel and vertical hake for depth; horizontal hake for width.

stem: A planter's seed plate turns once for every 3.0 m travelled and has 12 cells, each dropping one seed. Calculate the spacing between seeds in the row, in cm.
The same planter (3.0 m of travel per plate turn) must sow at 20 cm in the row. How many cells must the new seed plate have?
explanation: 3.0 m ÷ 0.20 m = 15 cells. Using 3.0 ÷ 20 without converting cm to m gives nonsense.
hints: Cells = distance per turn ÷ spacing (same units).

stem: An ox plough cuts a slice 30 cm wide at 2.5 km/h and ploughs for 75% of the working time. Calculate the hours needed to plough 0.9 ha.
Name the part of the plough that cuts the soil vertically ahead of the share on some (mainly tractor) ploughs.
explanation: The **coulter**.

stem: Describe the routine maintenance an ox plough should receive at the end of each day's work.

points.description: Scrape off soil and plant material.
Check and tighten loose nuts and bolts; replace missing ones.
Grease or oil the wheel bearing and other moving parts.
Inspect the share, point and heel for wear or damage and sharpen or report them.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: At the end of the day the plough is scraped clean, all nuts and bolts are checked and tightened, the wheel is greased, and the share and heel are checked so that blunt or worn parts can be sharpened or replaced.

explanation: Daily care.

stem: Suggest **three** reasons why a planter gives a better maize stand than sowing by hand behind the plough.

points.description: Seed is dropped at an even spacing, giving the intended plant population.
Seed is placed at a uniform depth and covered, so germination is even.
Fertiliser can be placed beside the seed at the same time / less seed is wasted and work is faster.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: A planter drops seed at an even spacing and a uniform depth and covers it, so the plants emerge together at the right population. It can also place fertiliser beside the seed, wasting less seed and saving time.

explanation: Precision of planters.
hints: Think of spacing, depth and fertiliser.

stem: A pupil describes an ox-drawn mouldboard plough: "At the front a chain is fastened to a metal piece with two rows of holes. A small wheel is fixed under the front of a long bar. At the back, a pointed steel blade at the bottom is followed by a curved plate. On the other side is a flat plate whose back end wears away. Two handles rise at the back."

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Name the metal piece with two rows of holes.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Name the pointed steel blade at the bottom.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Name the flat plate on the other side.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: State the function of the curved plate.

points.description: Lifts and turns (inverts) the furrow slice.
Buries weeds and crop residues.

parts.label: (f)
parts.stem: Explain why the back end of the flat plate is made as a separate, replaceable part.

points.description: It rubs on the furrow bottom and wears quickly.
Replacing only the heel is cheaper than replacing the whole landside.

explanation: Identify plough parts from a description and explain their functions.
hints: Match each description to a named part.

stem:
Farai checks his ox planter before planting maize. He pushes it 50 m along a hard path and counts 180 seeds dropped. He wants seeds every 25 cm.

| Fault seen | Likely cause |
| --- | --- |
| Plough rides out of the ground | ? |
| Rust on the mouldboard after storage | ? |
| Wheel squeaks and wobbles | ? |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the actual seed spacing, in cm, to one decimal place.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate how many seeds should have been dropped over the 50 m.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: What should Farai do to correct the spacing?

options.content: Fit a seed plate with fewer cells
options.rationale: That would widen the spacing further.

options.content: Fit a seed plate with more cells
options.rationale: Correct: more seeds per turn gives closer spacing.

options.content: Raise the wheel of the plough
options.rationale: The plough wheel has nothing to do with planter spacing.

options.content: Fill the hopper only half full
options.rationale: Hopper level does not change cell number.

parts.explanation: The planter drops too few seeds; a plate with more cells (or a changed gear) gives the 25 cm spacing.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Suggest a likely cause for each fault in the table.

points.description: Plough rides out: blunt or worn share/point (or wheel set too low / hitch too low).
Rust: stored without cleaning and oiling, or in the open.
Wheel squeaks and wobbles: bearing not greased / worn bearing or loose bolt.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Describe how Farai should store his implements at the end of the season.

points.description: Clean off all soil and fertiliser and repair or list worn parts.
Coat bright metal surfaces with used oil or grease and paint the frames.
Store under a roof, off the ground on blocks, away from livestock.

explanation: Calibrate a planter and diagnose and prevent implement faults.

stem: Nyasha has a span of oxen and must (i) plough a hard field with old roots, (ii) prepare a fine seedbed after ploughing and (iii) earth up her potatoes.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Suggest an implement for job (i) and give a reason.

points.description: A disc plough (or a mouldboard plough with a sharp share, after stumping).
Discs roll over roots and stones without breaking or blocking.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Suggest an implement for job (ii) and give a reason.

points.description: A spike-tooth (or disc) harrow.
It breaks clods and levels the soil to a fine tilth.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Suggest an implement for job (iii) and give a reason.

points.description: A ridger.
Its double mouldboard throws soil up to both sides, covering the tubers.

explanation: Choosing implements for tasks.
